questiontext.text: Which tool did Copernicus Browser replace in 2026?

generalfeedback.text: EO Browser (Sentinel Hub) was retired in March 2026; Copernicus Browser of the Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem (CDSE) offers the same tools – compare, timelapse, time series, custom scripts.

questiontext.text: What do you need before the Earth Engine Code Editor opens without an error?

generalfeedback.text: Earth Engine access is tied to a Google Cloud project. Noncommercial (education) registration is free but takes 20–30 minutes and is periodically re-verified.

answer.text: A Google Cloud project registered for Earth Engine (noncommercial use)

questiontext.text: Which Sentinel-2 processing level contains surface (bottom-of-atmosphere) reflectance?

generalfeedback.text: Level-1C is top-of-atmosphere reflectance; Level-2A adds the atmospheric correction (surface reflectance) and the SCL scene classification band. In Earth Engine: COPERNICUS/S2_SR_HARMONIZED.

questiontext.text: What is the SCL band of a Sentinel-2 Level-2A product?

generalfeedback.text: SCL (scene classification layer) codes each pixel; classes 3, 8, 9 and 10 are cloud shadow, medium and high probability cloud and cirrus – the classes masked in lesson 2.

answer.text: A per-pixel scene classification (cloud, shadow, water, vegetation …) produced by the atmospheric correction
The surface reflectance in the short-wave infrared

questiontext.text: What is the revisit time of the Sentinel-2 constellation at the equator?

generalfeedback.text: One Sentinel-2 satellite repeats every 10 days; with two satellites in the same orbit the revisit is 5 days (shorter at higher latitudes where swaths overlap). Landsat 8/9 together: 8 days.

questiontext.text: Which Sentinel-2 bands have a 10 m pixel?

generalfeedback.text: B2/B3/B4/B8 are 10 m, the red-edge bands, B8A and the SWIR bands B11/B12 are 20 m, B1/B9/B10 are 60 m. An index that uses B11 or B12 (MNDWI, NBR) is effectively a 20 m product.

answer.text: B2, B3, B4 and B8 (blue, green, red, broad NIR)

questiontext.text: Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 data are free and open for anyone, including commercial use.

generalfeedback.text: Copernicus data are distributed under a free, full and open licence. The constraint in this course is compute and account access, not data licensing.

questiontext.text: Which two accounts does the course require before lab 1? (select all that apply)

generalfeedback.text: Milestone M1: a CDSE account for Copernicus Browser and a Google account with a Cloud project registered for Earth Engine.

answer.text: A Google account with a registered Earth Engine project

category.text: $course$/top/AGeoHazard – final test/L2 Earth Engine basics and NDVI

questiontext.text: In Earth Engine, what is the difference between an ee.Image and an ee.ImageCollection?

generalfeedback.text: COPERNICUS/S2_SR_HARMONIZED is a collection of millions of scenes; filterDate / filterBounds select scenes, median() turns the collection into one ee.Image.

answer.text: An ee.Image is one raster with one or more bands; an ee.ImageCollection is a stack of images (e.g. all Sentinel-2 scenes)
An ee.Image is a single band; an ee.ImageCollection is a multi-band image
An ee.ImageCollection is an image downloaded to your computer

questiontext.text: In filterDate('2025-05-01', '2025-09-30') the end date is exclusive – scenes acquired on 30 September are NOT included.

generalfeedback.text: The end date of filterDate is exclusive; use the day after the last day you want.

questiontext.text: What does .filter(ee.Filter.lt('CLOUDY_PIXEL_PERCENTAGE', 35)) do?

generalfeedback.text: It is a scene-level filter on a metadata property. Per-pixel masking needs a cloud mask: SCL classes, Cloud Score+ (cs_cdf) or the QA60 bitmask (lesson 2, step 5).

answer.text: Removes whole scenes whose metadata says more than 35 % cloud – it does not mask any pixel
Masks every cloudy pixel in every scene
Keeps only pixels with less than 35 % cloud probability

questiontext.text: In the Cloud Score+ mask the rule image.select('cs_cdf').gte(0.6) keeps pixels …

generalfeedback.text: cs_cdf is a 0–1 clear-sky score: 1 = certainly clear. gte(0.6) keeps pixels with score ≥ 0.6; the collection is joined with linkCollection.

answer.text: … that are likely clear; a higher threshold (e.g. 0.65) is stricter, a lower one (0.5) keeps more pixels

questiontext.text: The Sentinel-2 QA60 cloud bitmask is reliable for all scenes in the archive.

generalfeedback.text: QA60 is unpopulated for scenes from 25 January 2022 to 28 February 2024. Use the SCL band or Cloud Score+ for that period.

questiontext.text: What does image.normalizedDifference(['B8', 'B4']) compute?

generalfeedback.text: normalizedDifference(A, B) = (A − B) / (A + B). With NIR = B8 and red = B4 it is NDVI, ranging from −1 to 1; dense vegetation > 0.4, water < 0.

answer.text: (B8 − B4) / (B8 + B4), i.e. NDVI for Sentinel-2

questiontext.text: What does s2MaskedCS.map(addNDVI) do?

generalfeedback.text: map() is the Earth Engine way of looping over a collection; nothing is computed until a result is requested (print, Map.addLayer, Export).

answer.text: Runs the function addNDVI on every image of the collection on the server and returns a new collection
Adds a layer to the map panel
Downloads the collection and runs the function locally
Runs the function on the median image only

questiontext.text: ndviCollection.median() returns …

generalfeedback.text: A reducer over time collapses the collection into a single image. The median is robust to the remaining clouds and shadows.

answer.text: … one ee.Image whose pixel values are the per-pixel median over time
… an ee.ImageCollection with half of the images
… a number: the median NDVI of the area
… the middle scene of the collection

questiontext.text: In reduceRegion, why must scale be 10 for Sentinel-2 rather than 1?

generalfeedback.text: The scale must match the data: 10 m for Sentinel-2, 30 m for Landsat. A too small scale oversamples and fails; a too large one smooths the result.

answer.text: scale is the pixel size in metres at which the computation runs; 1 m forces a hundred times more samples than real pixels and ends with "Too many pixels"
scale is the number of bands to use
scale is a multiplication factor for the result

questiontext.text: How do you get the area of a class in hectares in Earth Engine?

generalfeedback.text: ee.Image.pixelArea() gives each pixel its area in m²; ee.Reducer.sum().group({groupField: 1}) sums it per class code; 1 ha = 10 000 m².

answer.text: Sum ee.Image.pixelArea() (m² per pixel) over the class pixels with a grouped reducer and divide by 10 000
Export the image and read the file size

questiontext.text: A pixel has reflectance B8 = 0.40 and B4 = 0.10. What is its NDVI? (two decimals)
Which three operations form the skeleton of nearly every Earth Engine script in this course? (select all that apply)

generalfeedback.text: Load/filter → map → reduce; the same three verbs appear in Python, in the QGIS console and in openEO.

answer.text: Reduce the collection to one image (median) or a number
Download all scenes to the local disk

questiontext.text: In a pixel-based classification, what is the difference between a feature and a label?

generalfeedback.text: Each pixel is a row of a table: the bands and indices are the features (predictors), the land cover code is the label.

answer.text: A feature is an input column (a band value, an index, slope); the label is the class we want to predict
A feature is the class; the label is the pixel coordinate
A feature is a vector layer; a label is its name

questiontext.text: Which statement about Random Forest and k-means in Earth Engine is correct?

generalfeedback.text: ee.Classifier.smileRandomForest is supervised (labelled data); ee.Clusterer.wekaKMeans is unsupervised – you name the clusters afterwards.

answer.text: Random Forest needs labelled training pixels; k-means needs no labels and returns cluster ids
k-means needs labelled training pixels; Random Forest does not

name.text: L3-03 Cluster is not a class

questiontext.text: A k-means cluster number is a land cover class.

generalfeedback.text: k-means finds spectral groups. Sunlit and shaded forest may become two clusters, wheat and grass one. You must inspect the map and relabel clusters to classes before any accuracy can be computed.

questiontext.text: Why do you keep 30 % of the samples aside as a test set?

generalfeedback.text: randomColumn() and a 0.7 split give training and test sets; the confusion matrix is computed on the test set only.

answer.text: To measure the accuracy on pixels the model has never seen – otherwise the accuracy is meaningless
Because Earth Engine cannot train on more than 70 % of the samples

questiontext.text: A confusion matrix of 200 test pixels has 176 on the diagonal. What is the overall accuracy in percent?

generalfeedback.text: Overall accuracy = correctly classified / total = 176 / 200 = 0.88 = 88 %.

questiontext.text: What does producer's accuracy of the class crops tell you?

generalfeedback.text: Producer's accuracy = recall (omission errors); user's accuracy = precision (commission errors). Both are read from the confusion matrix.

answer.text: Of the real crop pixels, how many did the map find (recall)
Of the pixels the map calls crops, how many are really crops (precision)
The share of crops in the whole area
The number of training polygons for crops

questiontext.text: What does a kappa value of 0 mean?

generalfeedback.text: Kappa corrects the agreement for chance: 0 = random, 1 = perfect. Report overall, producer's and user's accuracy; kappa is optional (Foody 2020).

questiontext.text: When you draw training polygons in the Code Editor, how must the geometry layers be imported for sampleRegions to work?

generalfeedback.text: Import as Geometry gives no properties, so sampleRegions returns nothing useful. Use one FeatureCollection per class with the same property name and codes 0 … 3 everywhere.

questiontext.text: Which actions typically improve a Random Forest land cover classification? (select all that apply)

generalfeedback.text: Cloud masking, extra bands, more trees and better samples help; validating on the training pixels only inflates the accuracy.

answer.text: Masking clouds per pixel before taking the median composite
Adding spectral indices (NDVI, MNDWI, NDBI) and elevation/slope as bands
Training and testing on the same pixels

questiontext.text: What does classified.focal_mode({radius: 1, kernelType: 'square', units: 'pixels'}) do?

generalfeedback.text: The mode of the 3 × 3 neighbourhood replaces each pixel – post-processing that smooths the classified map.

answer.text: A majority filter that removes isolated salt-and-pepper pixels

questiontext.text: What is Dynamic World (GOOGLE/DYNAMICWORLD/V1)?

generalfeedback.text: Dynamic World (Google / WRI, Brown et al. 2022) does the lab 3 task with a neural network and is a convenient reference layer for your report.

answer.text: A near-real-time per-pixel land cover product from Sentinel-2 made with a convolutional neural network

questiontext.text: You added NDVI and slope to the image as stack = composite.addBands([…]) but the accuracy did not change at all. Most likely …

generalfeedback.text: Use stack.bandNames() in inputProperties and classify stack; classifier.explain() then shows the importance of the new inputs.

answer.text: … you still trained on composite.bandNames() and classified composite, so the model never saw the new bands
… the new bands are identical to the old ones
… Random Forest cannot use more than 6 bands
… the test set is too large

category.text: $course$/top/AGeoHazard – final test/L4 Floods – water indices and SAR

questiontext.text: Why does water appear dark in the near-infrared and short-wave infrared bands?

generalfeedback.text: This contrast is the basis of every water index: green (reflected a little) versus NIR or SWIR (absorbed).

answer.text: Water absorbs NIR and SWIR almost completely, while vegetation and soil reflect them strongly
The sensor is not sensitive to NIR over water

questiontext.text: Which formula is MNDWI for Sentinel-2?

generalfeedback.text: MNDWI (Xu 2006) replaces the NIR of NDWI (B3, B8) by SWIR (B11), which suppresses built-up areas that also reflect little NIR.

questiontext.text: Why is MNDWI often preferred to NDWI in flooded towns?

generalfeedback.text: NDWI cannot suppress the built-up signal; MNDWI can. Note that B11 is a 20 m band, so MNDWI is a 20 m product.

answer.text: Buildings reflect little NIR like water, but more SWIR than water – so MNDWI separates water from built-up areas
NDWI cannot be computed in Earth Engine

questiontext.text: Why is Sentinel-1 radar the main tool for mapping the flood peak?

generalfeedback.text: Optical data are good for the situation after the event and for permanent water; the peak itself falls between Sentinel-2 passes and under clouds.

answer.text: Its C-band microwaves (about 5.6 cm) pass through clouds and work day and night – the peak is usually under the clouds that caused it
It has a higher spatial resolution than Sentinel-2

questiontext.text: Why is calm water dark in a Sentinel-1 image?

generalfeedback.text: Typical VH values: water around −22 dB, land around −12 dB – a bimodal histogram that can be thresholded.

answer.text: Specular reflection: the smooth surface bounces the pulse away from the antenna, so very little backscatter returns (below about −18 dB)

questiontext.text: A flooded forest or a flooded street between buildings appears in SAR …

generalfeedback.text: Double bounce (water + vertical structure) increases the backscatter; it is one reason why flooded vegetation and urban floods are missed by the "water is dark" rule. VV reacts most.

answer.text: … brighter than before, because of double-bounce reflection between the water surface and trunks or walls

questiontext.text: In SAR change detection you may freely mix ascending and descending Sentinel-1 scenes in the before and after stacks.

generalfeedback.text: Never mix orbit directions: the viewing geometry differs, so the backscatter of the same pixel differs. Filter one orbit pass, one mode (IW) and one polarisation.

questiontext.text: Which polarisation does the lesson recommend for floods in open land, and why?

generalfeedback.text: VH (volume scattering from vegetation) gives a bigger contrast between land and open water; VV is better for flooded vegetation (double bounce).

answer.text: VV – it is the only one in the catalogue

questiontext.text: In the UN-SPIDER script the flood is where after_dB / before_dB exceeds 1.25. What does that mean?

generalfeedback.text: The dB values are already logarithms, so the ratio is a convention. A difference threshold in dB (e.g. −3 dB) does the same more transparently.

answer.text: The after value is at least 25 % more negative (e.g. −12 → −15 dB, about 3 dB darker); it is a ratio of dB values, not of physical backscatter

questiontext.text: Which masks does the UN-SPIDER flood script apply to the change layer? (select all that apply)

generalfeedback.text: JRC GSW removes lakes and rivers, the HydroSHEDS DEM slope mask removes shadow on slopes, connectedPixelCount removes specks. There is no built-up mask.

answer.text: Permanent water from the JRC Global Surface Water seasonality layer
Slopes steeper than 5° (radar shadow is not water)
Isolated groups of fewer than 8 connected pixels

questiontext.text: Why does the script apply a 50 m focal mean to the SAR images?

generalfeedback.text: Speckle must always be filtered before thresholding; the radius is a trade-off between noise and detail (sensitivity test: 30 m vs 100 m).

answer.text: To reduce speckle – the salt-and-pepper noise inherent to radar images

questiontext.text: Why does milestone M4 require the flooded area for thresholds 1.15, 1.25 and 1.40?

generalfeedback.text: A map whose area changes by less than a factor of two between the thresholds is robust; a large change means the threshold matters more than the data.

answer.text: To show the uncertainty of the map – how much the area depends on an arbitrary parameter

questiontext.text: What does SAR interferometry (InSAR) measure that backscatter analysis does not?

generalfeedback.text: Backscatter uses the amplitude (how much echo returns); InSAR uses the phase (how far it travelled). DEMs (SRTM, TanDEM-X → Copernicus DEM) and subsidence maps come from InSAR.

answer.text: The phase of the signal – giving topographic height and ground displacement with millimetre accuracy

questiontext.text: Which Earth Engine collection holds Sentinel-1 ground-range-detected backscatter, and in which unit?

generalfeedback.text: GRD = amplitude only, terrain corrected; the SLC products with phase are not in Earth Engine (CDSE has them – lesson 7, optional page).

answer.text: COPERNICUS/S1_GRD, values already in dB, 10 m pixels in IW mode

questiontext.text: What is a landslide?

generalfeedback.text: USGS definition. From orbit you see the scar (bare, bright source area), the track and the deposit.

answer.text: The downslope movement of soil, rock and organic material under gravity, and the landform that results from it
The erosion of a river bank by water

questiontext.text: In the Varnes (1978) scheme used by the USGS Landslide Handbook, landslides are classified by …

generalfeedback.text: Material: rock or soil (earth = fine, debris = coarse). Movement: fall, topple, slide (rotational or translational), flow, spread, complex.

answer.text: … the type of material (rock, earth, debris) and the type of movement (fall, topple, slide, flow, spread)
… the season in which they occur

questiontext.text: Which of the following is a trigger of a landslide, not a precondition?

generalfeedback.text: Preconditions answer "why here" (slope, lithology, land cover, road cuts) and are the predictors of a susceptibility model; triggers answer "why now" (rainfall, earthquakes, snowmelt).

answer.text: An old landslide on the same slope

questiontext.text: Which product answers the question "Where did landslides happen after event X?"

generalfeedback.text: Inventory (where did it happen), susceptibility (where could it happen), hazard/risk (how likely, how often, what is exposed). The lab produces an inventory-type heatmap – the input of everything else.

answer.text: An inventory – from before/after change detection or visual mapping

questiontext.text: What input does the landslide density heatmap method of Handwerger et al. (2022) use?

generalfeedback.text: Pre- and post-event stacks reduced to their medians, the log-ratio of the two, masks for flat terrain and water, the 99th percentile flagged and turned into a kernel density heatmap.

answer.text: Sentinel-1 SAR amplitude (VH) before and after the event, same orbit – no training data
Labelled training polygons and a Random Forest

questiontext.text: I_ratio = 10·log10(I_pre / I_post) = I_pre − I_post in dB. A strongly positive value means …

generalfeedback.text: A positive log-ratio = darker after the event. There is no absolute threshold; the paper uses the 99th percentile of the AOI.

answer.text: … the backscatter decreased after the event – vegetation removed, a fresh scar: a landslide candidate

questiontext.text: Which pixels does the heatmap script mask out? (select all that apply)

generalfeedback.text: Slope, curvature and water masks from NASADEM; there is no built-up mask, so urban change can appear in the heatmap.

questiontext.text: Why can a slow, creeping landslide not be mapped with the before/after method of the lab?

generalfeedback.text: Rain- or earthquake-triggered events give a sharp date; creep over years is an InSAR (phase) problem – lecture 5.

answer.text: There is no event date, so there is no sharp before/after pair; slow movement needs InSAR time series instead
Creeping landslides are invisible to all satellites

questiontext.text: What happens when you lengthen the pre-event Sentinel-1 stack from 2 to 8 months?

generalfeedback.text: More images → a smoother median; a too short stack gives a noisy, blocky heatmap everywhere.

answer.text: The pre-event median has less speckle noise, so the ratio is cleaner – at the cost of more seasonal mixing

questiontext.text: Where are about 95 % of the landslides of Poland?

generalfeedback.text: The SOPO inventory of the Polish Geological Institute holds more than 70 000 landslides (2023), almost all in the Carpathians.

questiontext.text: The Console prints an empty image collection for the post-event window. What should you do first?

generalfeedback.text: Sentinel-1 repeats every 6–12 days per orbit; a short window may contain no scene of the chosen pass.

answer.text: Widen the window or switch the orbit direction – there is no Sentinel-1 scene of that orbit in the window

category.text: $course$/top/AGeoHazard – final test/L6 Wildfires and burn severity

questiontext.text: What is the difference between fire intensity and burn severity?

generalfeedback.text: dNBR maps severity (after). Fire Radiative Power from thermal sensors is an intensity measure (during). Soil burn severity drives post-fire erosion and debris flows.

answer.text: Intensity is the energy released during the fire (kW/m, FRP); severity is the effect on the ecosystem measured after the fire
Intensity is measured after the fire, severity during

questiontext.text: Which of the three fire products needs a before/after image pair?

generalfeedback.text: Active fire: thermal emission during the fire (VIIRS 375 m, MODIS 1 km). Burned area: monthly reflectance change + hotspots. Severity: NBR pre minus NBR post.

questiontext.text: How does the reflectance of a forest change after a fire?

generalfeedback.text: The two bands move in opposite directions – exactly what NBR exploits.

answer.text: NIR drops (leaves gone), SWIR rises (char, ash, dry soil)

questiontext.text: Which formula is the Normalized Burn Ratio for Sentinel-2?

generalfeedback.text: NBR = (NIR − SWIR2) / (NIR + SWIR2); for Landsat 8/9 SR_B5 and SR_B7. The UN-SPIDER page uses B8A instead of B8 – both acceptable, state which.

questiontext.text: dNBR = NBR_pre − NBR_post. A strongly positive dNBR means …

generalfeedback.text: Positive = vegetation loss, negative = enhanced regrowth. By convention dNBR is often scaled × 1000.

answer.text: … loss of vegetation: the pixel burned
… a cloud in the post image

questiontext.text: A pixel has dNBR = 0.50 (500 on the × 1000 scale). Which USGS burn severity class is it?

generalfeedback.text: USGS classes: < −0.25 regrowth high; −0.25…−0.10 regrowth low; −0.10…0.10 unburned; 0.10…0.27 low; 0.27…0.44 moderate–low; 0.44…0.66 moderate–high; > 0.66 high.

questiontext.text: Why should a Sentinel-2 NBR map be exported at 20 m rather than 10 m?

generalfeedback.text: An index inherits the coarsest band it uses. Exporting at 10 m only resamples the 20 m information.

answer.text: B12 (SWIR2) is a 20 m band, so the index is effectively a 20 m product
Earth Engine does not allow 10 m exports

questiontext.text: Why is NBR preferred to NDVI for burn severity?

generalfeedback.text: NDVI difference remains a useful second opinion in grassland.

answer.text: NDVI saturates in dense forest and recovers quickly with grass; the SWIR2 band of NBR reacts to char and soil moisture and stays changed for months

questiontext.text: For an initial assessment, when should the post-fire image be acquired?

generalfeedback.text: An extended assessment uses the next growing season with the same phenology as the pre image and measures mortality rather than char.

answer.text: 1–4 weeks after containment: smoke gone, ash still there
The same day as the pre image

questiontext.text: Your dNBR map shows high severity everywhere, also far outside the fire perimeter. The most likely cause is …

generalfeedback.text: Low severity everywhere outside the perimeter instead points to a phenology difference between the pre and post dates.

answer.text: … a cloud in the pre-fire composite (bright, high NBR before → large drop); mask clouds per pixel and check the true-colour view

questiontext.text: The public UN-SPIDER script loads COPERNICUS/S2. Why does the course copy use COPERNICUS/S2_SR_HARMONIZED?

generalfeedback.text: Same sensor, same processing level, same band set for pre and post; never mix Landsat pre with Sentinel post without harmonisation.

answer.text: COPERNICUS/S2 is Level-1C top-of-atmosphere reflectance; the harmonised Level-2A surface reflectance is consistent with labs 2–5 and across the 2022 processing change

questiontext.text: What does EFFIS provide for your report?

generalfeedback.text: EFFIS (European Forest Fire Information System) and Copernicus EMS perimeters are the reference; FIRMS hotspots give the start and end dates.

answer.text: Burnt area perimeters for Europe (fires ≥ 30 ha, Sentinel-2 based since 2018) to compare with your dNBR perimeter

questiontext.text: What is the purpose of RdNBR = dNBR / √|NBR_pre|?

generalfeedback.text: The USGS thresholds were derived for US forests; RdNBR is fairer when vegetation density varies across the perimeter.

answer.text: To normalise for the amount of pre-fire vegetation, making forest and grassland comparable

category.text: $course$/top/AGeoHazard – final test/L7 APIs – Python, QGIS, CDSE

questiontext.text: What is an API in the context of Earth Engine?

generalfeedback.text: Earth Engine has one engine and several clients: JavaScript (Code Editor), Python (ee, also inside Colab and the QGIS plugin), R (rgee, community).

answer.text: A software interface through which programs (Code Editor, Python, QGIS plugin, R) talk to the same Earth Engine servers

questiontext.text: Which Earth Engine client libraries are provided by Google itself? (select all that apply)

generalfeedback.text: Python and JavaScript are official; rgee (active) and EarthEngine.jl (unmaintained since 2023) are community wrappers of the Python API.

questiontext.text: What must run at the start of every Colab session before any Earth Engine call?

generalfeedback.text: Use the project id exactly as in the Cloud console, not the project name.

answer.text: ee.Authenticate() once, then ee.Initialize(project='your-project-id') with the registered Cloud project id

questiontext.text: Which changes are needed when translating a Code Editor script to Python? (select all that apply)

generalfeedback.text: Server-side objects are identical; only syntax changes. Band names stay B4/B8 in Earth Engine (openEO uses B04/B08).

answer.text: true / false / null become True / False / None
Band names change from B8 to B08

questiontext.text: In Python, print(s2.size()) shows <ee.Number object> instead of 37. Why?

generalfeedback.text: Use .getInfo() for small values only; images and big collections go out through Export, never through getInfo().

answer.text: ee objects are server-side recipes; .getInfo() fetches the value from the server

questiontext.text: In Python, an if statement on an Earth Engine server object (for example: if s2.size() > 0) evaluates the real value.

generalfeedback.text: A Python if on a server object is always true – the object exists, its value is unknown until getInfo(). Use .getInfo() or server-side ee.Algorithms.If.

questiontext.text: What does geemap.js_snippet_to_py() do?

generalfeedback.text: The translator handles the syntax table of lesson 7; you fix what it missed (quoted keys, .And(), getInfo()).

answer.text: Translates a Code Editor JavaScript snippet into Python code that you still have to check and fix

questiontext.text: A layer added with Map.addLayer in the QGIS Earth Engine plugin …

generalfeedback.text: Two doors to a real file: Export Image to GeoTIFF in the Processing Toolbox (small areas) or Export.image.toDrive in the Code Editor / Python (large areas).

answer.text: … is streamed as tiles from Earth Engine: you can view and overlay it, but not measure it or run zonal statistics – export a GeoTIFF for that
… is a GeoTIFF on your disk

questiontext.text: Which CRS should you choose for an export covering Poland that will be measured in metres in QGIS?

generalfeedback.text: EPSG:4326 is in degrees (pixel size meaningless), EPSG:3857 inflates areas with latitude. Elsewhere use the UTM zone of the area.

questiontext.text: Hokkaido lies at about 142° E. Which UTM zone number is it? (zone = ⌊(longitude + 180) / 6⌋ + 1)

generalfeedback.text: (142 + 180) / 6 = 53.67 → floor 53 → zone 54; northern hemisphere → EPSG:32654.

questiontext.text: Where does Export.image.toDrive run and where does the file land?

generalfeedback.text: The plugin's Export Image to GeoTIFF instead downloads through your computer – fine for a few kilometres, not for a voivodeship.

answer.text: On Google's servers (Tasks tab / task.start()); the GeoTIFF appears in the Google Drive folder you named
On your computer; the file lands in Downloads
In QGIS; the file is added to the canvas

questiontext.text: What does the Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem (openEO, JupyterLab) offer that Earth Engine does not? (select all that apply)

generalfeedback.text: CDSE gives Copernicus data at the source and an EU-hosted, standards-based workflow; Earth Engine gives the catalogue, classifiers and free compute.

answer.text: An open standard API (openEO) that runs on several backends, no Google account

questiontext.text: In Colab, where must the %%R cell magic be placed?

generalfeedback.text: A cell magic (%%) must be the first line; a line magic (%R) runs a single line and can copy an R variable to Python.

answer.text: In the very first line of the cell
